Total 7.00 Jan. 1, 1919 Cushman 30 Disbursing Officer Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle Dillon, Mont. August 13, 1917 Dear Mr. Hammond, I reach Dillon alright and I was safe. Please let me know when school starts. I am feeling fine and hope your the same. How is Moses Miller getting along and the rest of the boys are they well. When school starts please send for me. How is the weather there? We had a little rain but not much. Your loving Friend, John Kinsh Miss soon or sooner good by. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Aug. 14, 1919 Mr. John Kinsh Dillon, Montana Dear John: I received your letter of August 10th and was glad to hear that you are enjoying good health and a pleasant vacation. Moses Miller is getting along just fine and the other boys seem to be well and happy. School begins September 2nd, and you may be sure that I shall send for you in plenty of time so that you may enter school on that date. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. /MG VACATION REQUEST FOR PUPIL. Willow Mont. We, the undersigned, respectfully request that leave of absence be granted ____________________________ John Kinsch from June 27th -1919 to Sept. 5th -1919 to enable him to visit his home. We hereby agree to pay all expenses, including round-trip railroad fares, sleeping-car fares, meals, lodging, stage fares, telegraph and telephone messages, and other incidental expenses connected with the visit. We further agree that said pupil shall be returned to the Cashman school on or before the last day of the leave of absence. We further agree to deposit with the superintendent of the school sufficient money to defray all expenses to be incurred, and should the pupils, or any one of them, fail to return to school at such time as may be agreed upon by the parents or guardian and the superintendent of the school in which the pupils are enrolled, the amount of money remaining with the superintendent, necessary to the return transportation of the pupil or pupils so neglecting to return, shall be forfeited to the Government; provided, however, that in all cases where it can be shown that there were justifiable reasons for the failure of the return of the pupil the forfeiture of the funds shall not take place. If the pupil neglecting to return is from a reservation, the superintendent of the reservation shall certify to the reasons for the nonreturn of the pupil or pupils. If a pupil's home is not on a reservation, then the certificate of some reputable, disinterested citizen of the community may be requested as to the reasons for the nonreturn of the pupil or pupils. --------------------------------------------------------------- Father. --------------------------------------------------------------- Mother. --------------------------------------------------------------- Guardian. Dillon, Montana September 14, 1919 Dear Sir: We received your letter and was glad to hear from you. When am I supposed to come to school? I wish you would write and let me know. Johnie's father is away fighting fire, and I wish you would let me know how I must send Johnie. We expect a letter from his father but haven't received none yet. Johnie goes every day on the Post Office to see if she got a letter from you. Johnie is awful anxious to get to school. My school starts Monday, and Don Johnie's little friend and he asked me to write for him. When the school commences let us know at once what I must do. I'm only fourteen years old but I'm so nice little friend and he is having a good time. Yours sincerely, Julia Bock Please send the answer in this name because he stays with us. Miss Julia Bock 589 Kentucky Ave. Dillon Montana. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Sept. 10, 1919 Mr. John Kinsch Dillon, Montana My dear John: I received the letter written by Miss Julia Bock, 589 Kentucky Avenue, Dillon, Montana. Since you live in town and can attend public school, I do not see how I can admit you again to Cushman unless your father is willing to pay the tuition fee of $200.00 a year. You are not a ward of the Government as your father is a white man and you live in a city possessing the necessary public school facilities. I shall send your check in the ordinary course of business. A copy of this year's booklet is sent you. Be sure to save it to show to Papa and draw his attention to rule No. 3. I am sorry I cannot receive you without the payment of a tuition fee. Sincerely yours, Superintendent. EHH:MC Cushman Indian School, Nov. 13, 1918. Mr. Thompson: The bearer is Mr. Kinsch who has just enrolled his son John Kinsch. Please see that they get dinner. Respectfully, Supt. Seattle Jan 7th Dear Son I have not heard from Julia yet. When I do I will let you know I am going to look as soon as the boat is finished. Be a good boy and have lots of fun. I got a telegram to come and see you I will and it should be long till October. Then I will have some time about forgot it I thought school started new year day. I will let down when I get one more from Julia. Good Bye John French 90's first av Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Sept. 19, 1919 Mr. John Kinsch Tacoma, Wash. The law provides: "That no part of this appropriation, or any other appropriation provided for herein except appropriations made pursuant to treaties, shall be used to educate children of less than one-fourth Indian blood whose parents are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they live and where there are adequate free-school facilities provided and the facilities of the Indian schools are needed for pupils of more than one-fourth Indian blood." (Act of August 1, 1914.) EXTRACTS FROM SCHOOL RULES. If the facilities of a school are not needed as provided in the above paragraph, children showing any Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, and who if debarred from Government schools could not obtain an education, may be enrolled in the day and boarding schools of their reservation; these children, however, may not be transferred to nonreservation schools without special permission from the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Before enrolling a pupil superintendents must satisfy themselves whether he has left any other school without permission and whether he has been expelled for cause from any other school. A pupil who has been expelled for cause from any Indian school may be reenrolled in any Indian school only with permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. "The Secretary of the Interior may in his discretion withhold rations, clothing, and other annuities from Indian parents or guardians who refuse to or neglect to send or keep their children of proper school age in some school during a reasonable portion of each year." Remarks: 5-297 n SHOE AND HARNESS REPAIRING. RECORD CARD—PREVOCATIONAL DIVISION. Each boy should devote five weeks to the work of this department during the three prevocational years. When he has accomplished the work as outlined in the course of study in a satisfactory manner, a suitable rating should be recorded. Ratings must be based on a practical application as well as a knowledge of the principles involved. Ratings should be excellent (E), good (G), fair (F). If pupil's work is not worthy of a rating of fair, no grade should be recorded. Under "Remarks" mention anything that indicates interest, conduct, and proficiency of the pupil.
